documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

Research on construction digitalisation has grown quickly but remains fragmented. This narrative review examines Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 2016 and 2025 on Building Information Modelling (BIM), artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, digital twins and related automation. A pool of 494 records was screened by title, abstract and keywords, and 89 articles were retained. An eligibility audit then separated 78 core studies from 11 records in which digital technology was contextual. The review combines a descriptive profile of the literature with an explicit, criteria based assessment of evidence maturity and of circular economy linkage. This narrative review used a single database and screening by one reviewer. Exclusion followed a construct based relevance test and not study quality. The exact date of the Scopus search was not recorded. Output accelerated after 2022 (74.2% of the 89 articles appeared from 2023 to 2025), 77.5% appeared in two MDPI journals, and author affiliations were concentrated in China and the United Kingdom. Nine overlapping themes emerged, led by BIM for design, coordination and compliance (39 core studies), robotics, automation and additive manufacturing (30), and AI and machine learning (24). Six records addressed circularity or waste reduction, and only two applied a digital tool to a material recovery or waste outcome. Within the retrieved sample, the link to the circular economy is therefore a thin evidence base and not an established finding, and the low count may partly reflect the search strategy. Case studies, pilots and cross sectional surveys are common (19 and 16 of the 89 screened records, respectively), whereas longitudinal studies and multisite validation appear limited. Blockchain evidence in the sample is minimal. A research agenda is proposed for validated, integrated and context-sensitive studies.

Generative artificial intelligence has destabilised an assumption embedded in copyright doctrine: that the person who communicates instructions to a machine is also the person who creates the resulting expression. This article examines where Sri Lankan copyright law should draw the line between AI-generated and AI-assisted literary and artistic works. Employing doctrinal and comparative methods, it analyses the Intellectual Property Act, No. 36 of 2003, leading Sri Lankan originality decisions and approaches adopted in the United States, the United Kingdom, the European Union and India. It argues that the statutory requirement of a physical-person author prevents attribution of authorship to an autonomous system, but does not preclude protection for sufficiently original human contributions embodied in an AI-mediated work. It proposes a five-stage Human Creative Contribution Test, proceeding through attribution, expressive specification, effective control and causation, originality, and protection and allocation. The proposed model avoids both automatic copyright for every prompt and indiscriminate denial of protection whenever AI has assisted a human creator. It further recommends evidential disclosure, clarification of partial protection and carefully framed statutory guidance rather than the immediate introduction of machine authorship.

Trust in artificial intelligence systems has become increasingly important as these systems assume advisory and decision-support roles. The present studies examine whether the temporal presentation of artificial intelligence (AI) generated responses, specifically typing animation speed, affects trust in chat-based interfaces. In Experiment 1, participants ( N = 71) interacted with three AI agents using pre-scripted question-response pairs detailing different facts about exotic animals. Response presentation speed (slow, fast, or instant) was manipulated within subjects. Results showed that compared to instant presentation, typing animations significantly increased trust in the AI agent but not trust in individual responses. Experiment 2 ( N = 68) employed similar procedures but used a live language model and allowed participants to generate their own questions. Under these more naturalistic conditions, presentation speed influenced both measures of trust, with typing animations consistently producing higher trust than instant presentation. These findings demonstrate that temporal presentation features can systematically shape trust judgments independent of content quality.

Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

documents.abstract: This concept paper explores the evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within foreign language education, specifically examining the transition from Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) to Intelligent Computer-Assisted Language Learning (ICALL). Current research indicates that AI technologies, such as Machine Learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP), are being utilized to provide personalized learning experiences, automated feedback, and sophisticated assessment tools. While these tools demonstrate significant pedagogical benefits, including improved language proficiency and increased learner autonomy, challenges remain regarding teacher preparation, technological reliability, and ethical implications. This paper proposes a framework to effectively integrate AI into pedagogy, repositioning the teacher as a facilitator and mentor in an AI-enhanced environment.

Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, fundamentally driven by the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm, rely on setting external objectives and iterative trial-and-error. When confronted with complex nonlinear problems containing noise and conflicting constraints, this paradigm inherently induces statistical smoothing and compromise, yielding black-box models that lack interpretability and out-of-distribution generalization. To address these limitations, this paper proposes the Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology, reconstructing the solving process into four irreversible stages: Deconstruction, Structure, Construction, and Solving. The method suspends a priori presuppositions to strip unit coupling, extracts rigid invariants inherent to the problem, constructs equivalent mappings anchored to these invariants, and executes the mapping directly to generate the solution. Evaluation metrics and experience are relegated to a posteriori verification. Demonstrated through cross-disciplinary practices including number theory, Hamiltonian systems, deep learning, and seismic inversion, this methodology transcends the statistical fitting bottleneck. Structure-Driven and Objective-Driven methodologies are complementary: when structure is sufficient, solutions are directly constructed; when lacking, it degenerates into the OD path.

Executives deciding enterprise modernization, legacy-system transformation, AI adoption, organizational restructuring, digital-infrastructure change, and cross-functional governance must weigh legal, financial, cybersecurity, procurement, opera-tional, and AI-governance questions that sit in separate functions. The central methods of this paper are GAIM-DF (Governance-Aware Institutional Modernization Decision Framework), a human-gated advisory process for these decisions, and Risk-Adaptive AI Governance Optimization (RA-GO v2), a risk-adaptive optimizer with mandatory governance gates, halt-safe feasibility, distributionally robust evaluation, and preference-information triage for scarce human review; an accountable human decides. As an optional architectural extension, we compu-tationally evaluate a multi-expert coordination layer that convenes specialist capabilities by context and consolidates constraints conservatively. Evidence is staged across four complementary pre-deployment approaches: analytical verification; retrospective historical-data analysis; comparative computational benchmark-ing against strong baselines; and scenario-based stress testing under distributional shift. Together they provide complementary pre-deployment evidence for high-stakes governance analysis. A systematic review of university and public-sector governance, with observational process-log analyses and RA-GO scenario stress tests, yields six principal findings: role coordination is associated with shorter approval and process times under supporting falsification checks; robust evaluation preserves tail-risk protection under distribution shift; preference-information triage concentrates human review where it most reduces modeled regret; and mandatory gates, an intensity floor, and a halt state are jointly consistent. The multi-expert benchmarks report accuracy, false-positive, latency, and token-cost trade-offs and routing failure modes relative to a strong Single-Agent baseline and to RA-GO alone. Shadow-mode piloting and a risk-adaptive Hybrid remain future work.

documents.abstract: Employers are adopting software that tracks activity, scores behaviour and flags deviations, and surveys suggest that half of U.S. workers already believe they are monitored. This study asks what such monitoring is associated with in the places where trust and psychological safety are formed. It assembles the published results of two Harris Poll surveys for the American Psychological Association (2,515 workers in 2023 and 2,027 in 2024), Gallup’s September 2026 study of trust in leaders’ use of employee data, and Gallup’s 2026 workforce surveys on AI, and analyses them with explicit effect-size formulas: risk ratios, Cohen’s h, random-effects pooling, population attributable fractions and implied-rate bounds. Across ten published contrasts, monitored workers fared worse on every outcome, with a pooled effect size of h = 0.36 (95% interval 0.22 to 0.49 after allowing for correlated outcomes) and substantial heterogeneity (I-squared 70 percent). They were nearly twice as likely to plan to leave within a year (39 versus 21 percent; risk ratio 1.86, 95% interval 1.56 to 2.21), which would correspond to about 30 percent of such intentions if the association were causal. Trust in leaders’ use of employee data is low (20 percent a great deal) and steeply related to concern (13 to 65 percent across trust levels); only 19 percent of employees have ever been told what is collected, and conversations raise both trust and concern. The evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported and partly drawn from press summaries, so the findings are associations. Purpose - This study examines how AI-enabled workplace monitoring relates to psychological safety, trust and strain, and what published evidence implies about the conditions under which monitoring is tolerated. Design/methodology/approach - The paper reanalyses published survey contrasts from the American Psychological Association and Gallup using effect-size formulas, random-effects pooling with a correlation adjustment, replication tests across survey waves, attributable-fraction calculations and implied-rate bounds, with sensitivity checks for assumed group sizes and design effects. Findings - Monitoring is associated with higher strain, lower perceived respect and trust, and exit intentions; effects are heterogeneous but consistently positive. Trust in data use is closely tied to engagement and concern, and transparency raises trust and concern together. Research limitations/implications - Group sizes and design effects are approximated, some sources are secondary, and the data are cross-sectional self-reports with no causal identification or direct measure of psychological safety in the monitoring contrasts. Practical implications - Employers should specify what is monitored and why, involve workers in setting limits, keep humans in decisions that affect people, and expect transparency to raise questions before it builds trust. Social implications - Monitoring that workers read as distrust may carry costs in strain and turnover that are not visible in productivity dashboards. Originality/value - The paper combines two decades of theory on trust and psychological safety with the most recent U.S. survey evidence on AI-era monitoring and quantifies the size, heterogeneity and sensitivity of the reported associations.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping manufacturing work, offering opportunities for employee empowerment while introducing psychological and organizational demands. Using selected PRISMA 2020 reporting items to describe search and study selection, this structured narrative review draws on a final corpus of 16 empirical studies to develop the Human–AI Resource Dynamics (HARD) framework, integrating Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model. A theory-informed narrative synthesis identifies two potentially coexisting pathways with uneven empirical support. The Bright Empowering Path links psychological availability, self-efficacy, positive appraisals, and task fit with proactive behavior and performance. The proposed Dark Depleting Path organizes distinct associations involving hindrance appraisal, AI anxiety, job insecurity, and surveillance-related autonomy loss, rather than one empirically validated depletion chain. Individual, organizational, and technological conditions shape these relationships. Evidence for empowerment is comparatively more consistent, whereas depletion findings remain heterogeneous and primarily observational. Methodological diversity, geographical concentration, and limited longitudinal evidence constrain causal and cross-contextual conclusions. HARD provides an AI-specific integrative framework for future empirical testing and human-centered AI implementation within Industry 5.0.

Antibiotic-induced liver injury (AILI) is a heterogeneous subset of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) that ranges from self-limited biochemical abnormalities to acute liver failure and chronic cholestatic or autoimmune-like disease. This narrative review critically evaluates clinical and mechanistic evidence across major antibiotic classes while retaining a drug-centered structure. Human HLA associations, drug-specific T-cell responses, delayed onset, and immune-rich histology support adaptive immunity as a unifying framework for many therapeutic-dose idiosyncratic reactions. Direct evidence, however, varies by drug. Linezolid toxicity and historical high-dose intravenous tetracycline injury are better supported as non-idiosyncratic mitochondrial exceptions. Reactive metabolites, oxidative stress, transporter effects, and inflammatory stress may initiate or amplify injury, but cytotoxicity-only, lipopolysaccharide/TNF-α, animal, and organ-on-chip models do not by themselves reproduce clinical idiosyncratic AILI. In practice, management still requires phenotype classification, exclusion of competing causes, structured causality assessment, prompt withdrawal when feasible, severity-based referral, and avoidance of rechallenge. Biomarkers, pharmacogenomics, patient-specific models, microphysiological systems, and artificial intelligence remain investigational and require validation in adjudicated antibiotic-exposed cohorts with tolerant controls.

Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.

This essay argues that the phone and the computer will merge into a single device. Earlier attempts, phones that turn into a computer when plugged into a screen, changed how almost no one works, because the phone had to run desktop apps designed for a mouse and keyboard. The author argues that AI agents change this: once the heavy lifting is something you ask for in plain words, it no longer matters which device you speak from, and the merging of devices follows from a change in how people communicate with machines. Drawing on his own need to reach his agents from anywhere, and on the phone app he built to talk to the terminals where they run, he describes the portable life: staying connected to one's work from any place. The essay examines why the computing power the average user needs is close to fitting in a phone, what still stands in the way (cooling, heat, battery life and the complexity of the processor), and how a foldable phone attached to a screen, a keyboard and a remote could work as a full computer.

The public line, the dialogues filed under Plato, forms the desire and the capacity to read. His pupil wrote dialogues too, now lost, and lecture notes that survive. The pupil's successor continued the research and inherited the books. The corpus divides by genre because three persons favoured three genres, and by audience because a school keeps its lectures for its students. The treatises refer to the dialogues because a pupil refers to his teacher. The Characters is a later handbook of types drawn from life and from the comic stage; its first type, the εἴρων, is a stock figure of comedy, and its proem is a later addition. English This preprint presents a testable functional and ergonomic hypothesis for Gallo-Roman dodecahedra. It proposes that a finger inserted through an undecorated aperture could have acted as an internal tactile stop while a coin was checked against another aperture. The paper distinguishes between gauging an individual coin and the less certain possibility of sorting several coins inside the object. It includes a geometric estimate using an idealized dodecahedron and outlines tests with replicas and measured discs. The analysis does not establish the historical use of the artifacts; it identifies a mechanism that can be tested physically. Given that the Serbian Tax Administration struggles to keep up the pace with the number of employees needed for the amount of work that has to be performed, the starting hypothesis is that AI tools should be used and developed by the Serbian Tax Administration as the outcome could be more tax revenue effectively collected. documents.abstract: The work-family interface and psychological recovery from work remained as two parallel topics for many years until scholars started to acknowledge that they are intertwined. In the present study, we advance knowledge on the field by carrying out the first meta-analysis on this topic. A total of 71 studies conducted across the globe were included. We explored whether all types of work-family interaction relate to recovery, and whether the strength of the relationships varies depending on type of recovery. Our findings show that three forms of work-family interaction are significantly related to recovery, namely work-family conflict (WFC), family-work conflict (FWC) and work-family facilitation (WFF). In the case of WFF, the strength of this relationship varies depending on how recovery is conceptualised. For instance, the association is particularly strong when recovery is defined in terms of perceived control over leisure time. From all types of work-family interaction, WFC is the most widely measured, whereas from all forms of recovery, psychological detachment from work seems the most popular. Although recovery has been considered a dynamic process, most of the identified studies are cross-sectional. Based on our results, we identify gaps and present a resource-based theoretical model to guide future research and practice.

The demolition phase is one of the least digitally integrated phases in the construction lifecycle, despite its significant environmental, safety, and economic implications. Though extensively studied in design, construction, and operation, the use of Building Information Modeling (BIM), the Internet of Things (IoT), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in demolition activities has been limited. This paper aims to present a theoretical framework for the integration of BIM, IoT and AI in demolition activities to improve data-informed decision-making and operational efficiency. A synthesis of the present literature on digital technologies in construction is developed to arrive at a conceptual framework. The framework proposes a closed-loop system for demolition, leveraging BIM as the information core, IoT for real-time sensing and data collection, and AI for intelligent analysis and decision-making support. The proposed framework classifies interactions into three phases: pre-demolition assessment, demolition execution and post-demolition assessment. It shows the various layers of data transmission and decision-making hierarchies, it also shows how technologies come together to enable real-time feedback and improved collaboration in demolition activities. The research offers a structured theoretical foundation for the digital transformation of demolition practices and can be the basis for subsequent empirical verification and practical application in sustainable and intelligent demolition management.

The world-building capacity of imaginative literature fosters artificial experience through characters who are artificial beings. Interacting with generative AI in natural language also creates a type of artificial experience through algorithmically simulated social cues. Neither type of artificial experience is real in the sense of actually existing, but these artificial experiences can feel authentic. When fiction portrays artificial experiences, it encourages metacognitive reflection. This essay is a meditation on artificial experiences, the bloody business of the human condition, and Gregory Mone’s short story “Bleed.” The short story depicts AI as a specter, as something that is neither fully alive nor inanimate. As the story’s sentient fridge grows increasingly human, its mimicry of human society-almost the same, but not quite-challenges traditional definitions of humanity. In our world, AI may no longer be fictional, but it is shaped by fiction.

documents.abstract: This essay examines AI’s transformative impacts through Adam Braver’s short story “According to Alice,” which explores the increasingly blurred boundary between artificial and human in today’s world. While Alice’s creative work speaks to the benefits of human-AI complementarity, her alienation and ennui in both her personal and professional lives underscore the importance of human creativity, collaboration, and agency. Growing concerns about AI in areas such as the labor market, education, and human relationships point to the need for AI that is human-centric and “proworker.” AI’s trajectory is not predetermined but rather needs to be determined by human design and choices at every level: individual, firm, country, and society at large.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Programming a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine can be challenging. Until now, Classic CNC programming assistants have helped to simplify this process; however, these assistants are generally limited to predefined operations, lack adaptability and often omit preparatory CNC steps. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and conversational agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) present a significant opportunity to enhance Classic CNC assistants. These technologies enable the development of more versatile solutions, capable of engaging in natural conversations through a prompt-based system. Aligned with this challenge, we present IkasToD, a Task-oriented speech-based Dialogue (ToD) assistant that leverages the language understanding and reasoning capabilities of LLMs, to support CNC operators during the preparatory steps of manufacturing orders. The IkasToD assistant engages in a closed-loop dialogue with the CNC manufacturer’s API to gather preparatory phase information, replying to operator queries, and generating plans to address complex, multi-query questions. These high-level plans based on decision trees extend the system model without the need to redesign the assistant interface. System’s performance is evaluated in a case study from the Elkartek project IKASPROD (Work partially supported by the Basque Government, grant no. KK-2023/00027.), using an in-house dataset with variable scenarios.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agents that translate user requests into sequences of local tool invocations. While prior cache-based side-channel attacks target the locally deployed models, they typically require the adversary to share model-related components or hardware resources with the victim's inference process. These assumptions do not apply to the predominant agentic settings, in which commercial LLMs execute on vendor-controlled infrastructure. We show that agentic execution exposes a more practical attack surface: although inference remains remote, tools are executed on the user's machine and commonly rely on shared system libraries. In this paper, we first systematically evaluate Flush+Reload and Prime+Probe for monitoring agentic tool invocations. Our evaluation across three hardware platforms shows that Flush+Reload enables accurate, real-time tool monitoring, whereas Prime+Probe, despite supporting cross-VM attacks, incurs prohibitive monitoring overhead and suffers from cache-set aliasing. We present ToolPulse, a cache-based side-channel eavesdropping framework against tool-using agents. We first design the Tool Recovery Attack to reconstruct an agent's tool-execution workflow. We evaluate the Tool Recovery Attack on 11 LLMs across Codex and Claude Code. It consistently reconstructs tool workflows, with the lowest F1 score exceeding 93%. We further demonstrate two attack scenarios enabled by the recovered traces. Task Profiling Attack infers user intent across two Terminal-Bench task categories and the Trigger Localization Attack identifies sensitive tool calls in encryption/decryption and model training/inference workloads. Even under substantial system noise on a server shared by approximately 20 users, both Task Profiling Attack and Trigger Localization Attack maintain high accuracy.

Maintaining the quality and quantity of cereal grains is fundamental to global food security. However, persistent post-harvest losses caused by insects and vertebrate pests, storage molds, and environmental variability continue to threaten grain availability and safety. Conventional storage systems, which require routine inspection and chemical intervention, are challenged by climate change, emerging pests, and growing demand for safe and sustainable food. This review critically evaluates recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT)-based sensors, machine learning (ML), multimodal sensing, decision-support systems, climate-controlled storage, and reduced-risk pest management strategies, with an emphasis on their integration into predictive management systems. The effectiveness of sustainable management strategies, including hermetic storage, biopesticides, diatomaceous earths (DEs), and semiochemical-based approaches, is evaluated with an emphasis on efficacy, scalability, and practical feasibility, focusing on risk-based rather than blanket interventions. Based on these advances, the review proposes a six-stage conceptual framework encompassing the sensing of storage conditions, data analysis, risk prediction, decision-making, targeted intervention, and outcome verification. The central theoretical contribution is the development of a conceptual framework that integrates digital monitoring, climate risk assessment, and sustainable pest management. The framework provides practical guidance for storage managers to identify new risks, choose suitable actions, and assess management outcomes. Major constraints include limited datasets, sensor accuracy, model transferability, interoperability, and cost-effectiveness in smallholder systems. Future priorities include advancing edge and explainable AI, digital twins, and other technologies such as multimodal sensing and low-cost smart storage solutions for resource-constrained regions. Integrating digital technologies, climate adaptation, and sustainable pest management could enable adaptive, predictive stored grain management, reducing post-harvest losses, improving grain quality and safety, and strengthening global food security.

Solvent-resistant membranes (SRMs) enable energy-efficient molecular separations critical to petrochemical, pharmaceutical, fine chemical, and food processing industries, yet their environmental cost remains poorly addressed. Conventional SRMs are predominantly derived from nonrenewable petroleum-based polymers, fabricated using toxic organic solvents and stabilized through chemical cross-linking agents that generate hazardous waste streams. At end-of-life, the absence of viable recovery or recycling pathways further imposes a heavy environmental burden. With growing emphasis on environmental sustainability and circular economy, advancing high-performance, stable, and sustainable SRMs has become a pressing priority. Guided by the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry as an organizing framework, this Review critically examines recent advancements in sustainable SRMs development across three major directions: (1) green membrane materials, including biobased materials, degradable polymers, and low-impact environmentally friendly cross-linkers, (2) green fabrication processes, including alternative green solvents and environmentally friendly fabrication techniques, and (3) lifecycle-oriented strategies, including degradable and recyclable membrane design as well as artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)-guided membrane design and performance prediction. By integrating material innovation, process engineering, and lifecycle considerations within a unified green chemistry lens, this Review highlights pathways for developing next-generation, high-performance SRMs with reduced environmental footprint. It further outlines key challenges and opportunities for translating sustainable membrane technologies into industrial practice, supporting cleaner manufacturing and circular-separation technologies.

Secondary education systems across the Global South have adopted competency-based curricula that expect learners to construct knowledge, solve authentic problems, collaborate and demonstrate skills, yet large classes, teacher shortages and limited resources constrain the learner-centered pedagogy that these reforms require. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been proposed as a means of closing this gap, but its pedagogical role in competency-based education has not been systematically theorized. Guided by Vygotsky’s social constructivist theory, this study synthesized peer-reviewed and institutional literature published between 2015 and 2025 through a systematic review of 300 sources, selected from 12,125 Scopus and Web of Science records and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. The study found that competency-based reforms were constrained by teacher preparation, assessment practices and resources. GenAI offered affordances for scaffolding, dialogue, feedback, authentic task design and teacher support, and randomized trials in Nigeria and Ghana reported meaningful learning gains when GenAI tutoring was structured and supervised. However, unguided access was associated with overreliance and weaker independent performance, and connectivity, language, cost, teacher capacity and policy gaps constrained equitable use. The study proposes the Scaffolded Generative AI for Competency-Based Education (SGAI-CBE) framework, which organizes GenAI use into a six-phase pedagogical cycle anchored in the zone of proximal development, teacher-mediated scaffolding, collaborative knowledge construction, authentic assessment and the gradual fading of AI support, and situates the cycle within enabling conditions and guardrails appropriate for resource-constrained schools.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular personal assistants for language learning purposes. While exhibiting impressive capabilities on various Natural Language Processing tasks, including text summarisation, paraphrase generation, and question answering, their capacity to provide language learners with pedagogically adequate feedback is less clear. This is due, among other causes, to the lack of annotated data. In this paper, we describe a framework which aims at bridging this gap by (i) collecting manually annotated LLM-generated answers to learners' queries, and (ii) using this data to automatically characterise LLM skills along pedagogical dimensions with respect to a taxonomy of self-regulated LLM uses by language learners. This framework has been used to assess the ability of contemporary mainstream LLMs to generate pedagogically adequate answers to L2 French learners. Preliminary results on a small manually annotated dataset (N = 49) show that establishing a definitive assessment of these models remains elusive; rather, they reveal an absence of consensus among human experts when evaluating models.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for legal tasks, including legal research, drafting documents, and even for legal decision-making. As for other sectors, the use of GenAI in the legal domain comes with various risks and benefits that need to be properly managed to ensure implementation in a way that serves public values and protects human rights. While the EU mandates risk assessment and audits before market introduction for some use cases (e.g., administration of justice), other use cases do not fall under the AI Act’s high-risk classifications (e.g., legal consultation). Further, current risk management practices prioritise expert judgement on risk factor identification and prioritisation without a corresponding legal requirement to consult with affected communities. Seeing the societal importance of the legal sector and the potentially transformative impact of GenAI, the acceptability and legitimacy of GenAI solutions also depend on a better understanding of the risks and benefits citizens associate with the use of GenAI and under which conditions citizens find the use of GenAI in the legal domain acceptable. As a response, this paper presents data from a representative sample of German citizens ( n = 488) outlining citizens’ perspectives on the use of GenAI for two legal tasks: legal consultation and legal mediation. Concretely, we (i) systematically map risks and benefit factors for both legal tasks, (ii) describe predictors that influence risk acceptance of the use of GenAI for those tasks, and (iii) highlight emerging trade-off themes that citizens engage in when weighing up risk acceptability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Large language models increasingly rely on extended reasoning traces, yet the training signals used to shape this behavior remain coarse. Supervised fine-tuning on full trajectories forces the model to imitate an entire demonstration, overconstraining its output distribution, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning provides only weak credit assignment, rewarding or penalizing whole completions without identifying where they succeed or fail. We propose edit-based training, a general framework for learning from a model's own trajectories via localized textual corrections. Given a sampled completion, an editor identifies the first point of failure under a specified criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span. The model is then supervised only on these edited spans. By design, this concentrates supervision where the model's reasoning first breaks down and aims to preserve its existing reasoning patterns elsewhere. The method applies both offline and online, with the latter continually adapting supervision to the model's evolving failure modes. We instantiate this approach on reasoning instruction following with Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark. Compared to full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level reinforcement learning baselines, edit-based training substantially improves compliance with the reasoning instruction while largely preserving the model's skills on untargeted tasks. These results suggest that localized correction is an effective complement to these approaches for shaping how LLMs reason.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can support students throughout the academic writing process, and its responsible use requires skills in formulating prompts, verifying information, and checking references. This community engagement activity aimed to describe the implementation and outcomes of a three-hour AI training session for 45 Diploma III midwifery students at STIKES Namira Madina on November 12, 2026. Master’s students from UIN Syekh Ali Hasan Ahmad Addary Padangsidimpuan delivered the training through presentations, discussions, demonstrations, and hands-on exercises using ChatGPT, Gemini, and NotebookLM. The exercises covered selecting research titles, formulating research questions, developing research matrices, outlining proposals, preparing presentation slides, refining academic language, and finding and verifying references. The evaluation drew on interviews with all participants, observations during the exercises, and activity records. All participants reported that the training helped them prepare for their final assignments. Facilitators observed that approximately 75% of participants could independently use AI to support the preparation of the initial sections of a research proposal and could practice verifying journal references. Challenges included difficulties in formulating prompts and verifying information and references, limited access to laptops, and internet connectivity problems. The evaluation suggests that academic writing training should combine hands-on AI use with facilitator guidance and explicit instruction in verification to promote critical and responsible use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose: This paper presents TriageGPT for DataOps, an architecture in which large language model agents classify data pipeline incidents, retrieve relevant context, and perform constrained autonomous remediation, in order to reduce the manual triage effort that drives incident duration and on-call fatigue. Methodology: TriageGPT combines a retrieval-augmented classification agent that assigns alerts to a data pipeline specific incident taxonomy, a tool-use resolution agent that invokes actions from a vetted, blast-radius-tiered action library, and an audit-logged guardrail layer that gates and can automatically roll back actions, paired with confidence-based human-in-the-loop escalation. We describe the architecture, algorithms and calibration policy, map the design to safety and governance guidance, and report a prototype evaluation on a benchmark pipeline with a fourteen-category taxonomy, 2,800 labeled synthetic incidents and a twelve-week comparative deployment trial. Findings: TriageGPT achieved 94.3 percent top-one classification accuracy and 95.1 percent factual attribution accuracy with retrieval, against 68.4 percent without it. It resolved 71.5 percent of test incidents without human intervention at an incorrect-action rate of 0.6 percent, every one of which the guardrail caught and reversed. In the deployment trial it reduced median time to resolution from 41 minutes under manual on-call practice to 9.8 minutes. Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: For theory, the paper treats autonomous remediation as something earned through calibrated confidence and bounded blast radius rather than assumed. For practice, it provides an architecture, algorithms and evaluation method for resolving routine pipeline incidents while deferring the rest to a human with an evidence-grounded case. For policy, it maps autonomous remediation to existing guidance, informing how organizations set guardrails, audit requirements and risk tolerance for AIOps agents.

This concept paper addresses ecosystem-level trust for AI agents: what evidence entities need in order to trust each other, and how it can be produced and conveyed. We argue that, as with people, trust is a risk decision on an interaction, based on a variety of information collected in several steps over time. Some of this information is associated with the entities, some with the content and context of the interaction. Unlike people and organisations, digital entities are poor accumulators of trust (ephemeral, mutable, duplicable). Trust in digital entities therefore relies more on the durable entities connected to them (principal, operator, execution environment) and on the content and context of the interaction itself. We also discuss how far this evidence can itself be trusted, and outline directions for further work.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.

documents.abstract: Genosoils are minimally disturbed reference states within pedogenons, that is, soil units shaped by similar pedogenic processes within the Soil Security framework. They are central to assessing human impacts on soil functions, services, and resistance to threats. Large scale genosoil delineation currently relies on Human Modification Index (HMI) classifications, identifying areas where human modification is on the lower end of the spectrum. In intensively managed landscapes, there may be a lack of genosoils, presenting a problem in studying the condition of soil without a local reference state available. Because similar pedogenic processes may give rise to soils under the same pedogenon classification across geographically distant regions, non-local occurrences may provide an alternative source of reference information. Using the United Kingdom as a case study, we tested whether spatial embeddings (vectorised representations of land surface properties derived from satellite imagery) can detect genosoil signatures at 10 m resolution and whether these signatures can be transferred to regions with limited or absent local low-human-modification examples. We evaluated two satellite foundation-model embedding products, AlphaEarth and Tessera, across three contrasting pedogenons selected from the Global Pedogenon Map. Within each pedogenon, pixels with lower HMI values were generally more similar to the candidate genosoil reference, indicating that the embeddings capture a consistent reference signature in areas with low human modification. At the global scale, similarity to the UK genosoil was largely confined to biogeographically coherent regions. Cross-border substitution of local UK genosoil delineation was mostly limited, with meaningful partial recovery observed primarily in the highly modified agricultural pedogenon. These results indicate that satellite foundation-model embeddings can support higher-resolution genosoil delineation than is currently possible from global human modification products alone, extending the operational framework from 90 to 10 m.

Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT are now part of how many university students study, but we still know little about how students outside English departments use them to learn English. This exploratory survey looked at engineering students taking a non-major English course at a technical university in northern Bangladesh. Sixty-three students answered an online questionnaire with closed and open-ended items on how they use ChatGPT, what benefits they see and what problems they face. Use was very common: 96.8% had used ChatGPT, 55.6% used it daily and 54.0% used it often or always for English-related tasks, mainly for writing help, assignment preparation and generating ideas. Most students agreed that ChatGPT is easy to use (76.2%), gives useful explanations (73.0%) and saves time (71.4%). At the same time, 76.2% said its answers are not always accurate or relevant, 74.6% wanted more guidance on using it, and 66.7% reported that poor internet access limits regular use. More than half (57.1%) held both views together, finding the explanations useful and the answers unreliable. Students who used ChatGPT more often for English reported greater benefits (ρ = .41) and more over-reliance (ρ = .38), but they were no more likely to notice unreliable output (ρ = −.14). Only 39.7% preferred asking ChatGPT to asking a teacher. Open-ended answers pointed to wrong answers, language that is too advanced, and difficulty writing prompts. Because the sample is small, drawn from one institution and based on self-report, the findings describe students’ experience and not measured gains in proficiency. They suggest that these students need help in judging ChatGPT’s output more than they need encouragement to use it.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly transforming cinematic pre-production by enabling the efficient creation of high-quality concept art. Despite major advances in image generation models, limited research has examined how users cognitively and emotionally evaluate AI-generated cinematic imagery. This study investigated user acceptance of concept art generated by Midjourney v5.2 within East Asian science-fiction and fantasy film contexts through a multi-dimensional perceptual framework. A total of 384 participants, including both design professionals and non-design participants, evaluated AI-generated scenes across five cinematic categories. The proposed framework examined five perceptual dimensions: visual reasonability, narrative potential, aesthetic appeal, immersion, and overall acceptance. Reliability analysis and principal component analysis provided preliminary evidence for the internal consistency and coherent component structure of the measurement instrument. Multiple regression analysis revealed that all four perceptual constructs significantly predicted overall acceptance (R 2 = 0.275, p < 0.001). Among them, visual reasonability emerged as the strongest predictor (β = 0.217), followed by aesthetic appeal (β = 0.187), narrative potential (β = 0.175), and immersion (β = 0.151). Formal moderation analysis further identified expertise-related differences in the predictive roles of selected perceptual dimensions. Visual Reasonability and Immersion were more strongly associated with Overall Acceptance among non-design participants, whereas the effects of Narrative Potential and Aesthetic Appeal did not differ significantly between the two groups. Within the present Midjourney v5.2 and East Asian study context, these findings provide empirical evidence for the perceptual factors associated with user acceptance of AI-generated cinematic imagery and contribute a user-centered basis for further evaluation of human–AI collaborative workflows.

The lack of trust in artificial intelligence (AI) slows its adoption across industries and society, usually due to limited understanding of how AI works and its advantages, and of how its trustworthiness including its ethical impact are approached during development. Designing and validating a reliable AI system is complex, requiring inputs from various stakeholders throughout the development process. Ensuring that their concerns are systematically addressed remains a challenge. In this paper, a Value Sensitive Design (VSD) based approach to AI trustworthiness including ethics is presented. The rationale of VSD is that since technologies should primarily serve societal needs, the social impact and associated ethical problems should be anticipated by involving stakeholders at the earliest possible stage [ 1 ]. This paper presents a values reference model (VRM) and an implementation method (IM) for Trustworthiness Including Ethics (TIE) defined based on the VSD rationale mentioned. Also, the piloting of the VRM-TIE and of part of the IM-TIE in a use case involving collaborative robots is presented, addressing both technical and human-related characteristics of the AI systems. The preliminary findings in the work suggest that: (1) AI Trustworthiness is a broad concept that must be analysed in detail, considering the industrial context and other priorities, (2) Achieving a shared understanding among stakeholders is essential but difficult, highlighting the need for a structured dialogue, (3) Adopting this VSD based approach, composed by VRM-TIE and IM-TIE, may have a significant impact on the stakeholders’ minds.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Clinical large language models are usually judged by whether the final answer is right. Yet a model can reach a fluent, plausible output through invalid reasoning that static benchmarks do not detect, and confident hallucination, causally invalid inference, and spurious demographic shortcuts can pass conventional evaluation. This critical review covers four paradigms in turn: how clinical hallucination arises and why static metrics miss it; the agentic hallucination cascade, in which multi-agent and tool-augmented systems propagate and amplify early reasoning errors; process reward modeling as step-level supervision; and neuro-symbolic grounding, in which formal logic engines, ontology reasoners, and knowledge graphs place verifiable constraints on neural output. Within their encoded domains, systems with symbolic veto layers offer guarantees that hold relative to their encoded knowledge, and they report large gains on the safety measures they use. These results come from single studies, mostly in simulated or small-sample settings, and are not directly comparable with neural baselines. Process reward models remain bounded by the statistics of their training data. We propose a conceptual framework that maps each agentic failure mode to a symbolic intervention point, and we argue that clinical AI safety depends substantially on system architecture. Because current regulation emphasizes performance and does not require verification of reasoning steps, we argue that responsible certification should also audit reasoning trajectories alongside accuracy on static benchmarks.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Verification of One Detail Transferred to an Unchecked Interpretation, a mechanism by which checking one part of an account lends certainty to a wider interpretation even though the evidence for that interpretation stays the same. The paper asks which alternatives a check can distinguish. A finding can support a wider claim when it rules out a rival explanation. Where either explanation would have produced the same result, the choice between them remains open. In 2002, researchers dated the parchment of the Vinland Map to about 1434. A medieval drawing and a modern drawing on that same sheet would both yield the same parchment date. In 2003, a report in Hayadan placed the drawing about fifty years before Columbus’s voyage. The report offered a separate argument about the ink for its claim of authenticity, but gave no independent date for the drawing. In 2021, Yale reported finding modern ink throughout the map’s lines and text. In September 1904, a Berlin commission ruled out deliberate signaling under the conditions in which it examined the horse known as Clever Hans. Carl Stumpf, a commission member, later wrote that many readers understood the report as a declaration that the horse could think. Follow-up experiments by Oskar Pfungst and his colleagues identified an explanation the September examination had left open. Hans responded to small, unintended movements by a person he could see. Part of the Sources and Evidentiary Limits series within On Human Modeling, the paper places this mechanism alongside Tversky and Kahneman’s work on the conjunction fallacy. In a human–AI setting, a reviewer might verify that an assistant quoted a motion exactly from meeting minutes. The same wording could appear whether the motion passed or failed. Verifying the assistant’s further claim that the committee adopted it would require the recorded outcome.

AI platforms are becoming a major gateway to news and current events. This shift risks amplifying existing geographical biases that favour narratives from wealthier countries over those from the Global South. This is particularly relevant in Latin America, which accounts for the largest share of AI usage in the Global South. We examine how information about Latin America changes when users shift from conventional search engines to LLM-based search. We construct a dataset of 1,901 current events across nine Latin American countries, craft realistic queries, and submit them to three search engines and four language models. We vary query language and user location to represent local, diaspora, tourist, and foreign user scenarios. Across 49,207 requests and 8,834 unique domains, language models return a less diverse set of news sources than search engines. Across user types, the share of domestic news returned by language models is inconsistent. For local users, while search engines already return only 41.3\% local news, language models return a further 3.6 to 11.6 percentage points less. Taken together, our findings suggest that LLM-based search can reproduce and, in some settings, amplify geographical hierarchies in the reach and visibility of news sources. We release an open dataset to support multilingual and geographically diverse evaluation of LLM-based search, and highlight implications for more equitable information systems design.

documents.abstract: Human-centered artificial intelligence (HCAI) seeks to orient AI toward human values, autonomy, oversight, safety, and meaningful control. Yet the term “human-centered” leaves a prior question unresolved: what conception of the human is being centered? Much HCAI discourse approaches the human as user, decision-maker, rights-holder, stakeholder, or bearer of preferences and values. These conceptions are indispensable but incomplete. This article argues that HCAI must also recognize the human as an aesthetic subject: a being whose perception, attention, imagination, interpretation, and judgment are formed through experience. As recommendation, personalization, generative AI, and predictive systems increasingly organize the conditions under which people encounter and evaluate the world, AI can participate in forming rather than merely serving human preferences. The article develops the concept of aesthetic agency to describe the human capacity to participate meaningfully in the formation of one’s perceptual, imaginative, interpretive, and evaluative relation to the world. It distinguishes choice from judgment, preference from taste, generation from imagination, and optimization from experience. On this basis, it proposes an aesthetically expanded HCAI organized around openness, plurality, reflectivity, and transformability. To center the human is not only to preserve control over AI, but to preserve the capacity to perceive, imagine, judge, and become otherwise.

documents.abstract: UNSTRUCTURED: Transparency, explainability, and interpretability are ubiquitous in the health artificial intelligence (health AI) literature, yet are used inconsistently and often interchangeably. This Viewpoint does not attempt to define the three terms. It asks a prior, meta-level question: what kind of claim do we make when we call a system transparent, explainable, or interpretable? I argue that the three terms pick out three different kinds of claim. A transparency claim is structural: it concerns what can be inspected about a system. An explainability claim is relational: it concerns whether understanding is successfully conveyed to a specified class of observer. An interpretability claim is functional: it concerns whether a bounded human agent can, in principle, re-derive the system's output by following its procedure. I use the framing example of a clinical decision support system that uses machine learning to identify patients at risk of deterioration. I develop each claim type through competing technical accounts, consider salient objections to each, and defend the taxonomy against them. I close by drawing out what the taxonomy implies for the design, evaluation, reporting, and regulation of health AI, and for physician autonomy at the point of care.

documents.abstract: Purpose Novice university teachers often start without any formal preparation or education in teaching. This means that they develop their competencies through hands-on teaching experiences. These new and unfamiliar experiences can create tensions. Previous research suggests that tensions may provide opportunities for professional growth, but offers little understanding of how this learning process unfolds. Building on theories of workplace learning, this study aims to explore when and how novice university teachers’ tensions may lead to learning by identifying key antecedents, learning activities and learning mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal multiple case study was conducted including eight junior lecturers. Data were collected via weekly diaries and semi-structured interviews at the beginning and end of the academic year 2023-2024, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings The results show that novice university teachers learning from tension depends on a complex interplay between tension characteristics (e.g. intensity), individual antecedents (e.g. perfectionism, self-doubt) and contextual antecedents (e.g. social support). Together, these antecedents enabled or inhibited engagement in learning activities (e.g. collegial conversations), which ultimately fostered diverse learning outcomes through mechanisms such as perspective-taking or social validation. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for higher education policymakers and developers of professional development programs on how to foster supportive learning environments for novice university teachers. Originality/value This study offers in-depth insights into when and how novice university teachers learn from workplace tensions. By linking general theories of workplace learning to the study of tensions, it sheds light on the antecedents, activities and mechanisms that contribute to novice university teachers’ learning from tensions.

Pathology foundation models supply strong representations for whole-slide image classification, yet the confidence attached to their predictions remains hard to trust. Prevailing uncertainty estimators act within a single feature space and thereby overlook the uncertainty that the choice of foundation-model representation itself induces. This work introduces CALIFUSE, a calibration-oriented framework that fuses several pathology foundation models for the specific purpose of uncertainty estimation. Departing from accuracy-driven fusion, CALIFUSE reads representational heterogeneity across encoders as an explicit confidence cue. Slide-level decision consensus is coupled with chunk-level evidence agreement quantified through Jensen-Shannon divergence, so that both prediction stability and fine-grained evidence consistency inform the estimate. Foundation-model encoders stay frozen. A task-specific nnMIL classifier is still trained for each FM; CALIFUSE then estimates confidence at inference without training an extra fusion module. Evaluated on seven WSI classification tasks under several foundation-model combinations, the framework sharpens calibration, misclassification detection, and selective prediction relative to both the strongest single-encoder baseline and naive ensemble averaging, all while preserving competitive balanced accuracy.

documents.abstract: Image-guided navigation supports operative planning, instrument localisation and trajectory control in cranial, stereotactic and spinal neurosurgery. Its reliability, however, depends on the continued validity of registration, tracking and anatomical correspondence throughout the procedure. Navigation discordance may arise when these relationships change, and the discrepancy may not be immediately apparent from the navigation display alone. This critical narrative review examines the mechanisms of navigation discordance, methods used to verify suspected inaccuracies, and strategies that may support recovery across cranial, stereotactic and spinal procedures. Particular attention is given to the distinction between registration accuracy, final technical accuracy, workflow reliability and clinically meaningful outcomes. The review also considers intraoperative MRI, intraoperative ultrasound, stereotactic verification, spinal navigation, augmented reality and human factors relevant to the recognition of unreliable guidance. Based on a structured synthesis of the literature, we propose a five-stage response framework comprising detection, pausing image-dependent action, independent verification, recovery and documentation. We also propose a minimum reporting dataset for navigation-related interruptions to improve consistency in the description of discordance, corrective actions and their consequences. The proposed framework is conceptual and has not undergone formal expert consensus, prospective usability testing or clinical outcome validation. It is intended to support discussion, local protocol development, reporting and future research rather than serve as a validated clinical algorithm. More consistent reporting of navigation interruptions and recovery processes may improve understanding of how image-guided systems perform under real operative conditions.

Restorative justice (RJ) places considerable emphasis on dialogue. Yet when dialogue is understood primarily as spoken exchange, the potential of the body as a medium of expression, response, and understanding can be overlooked. Taking the Japanese work WIND BREAKER, first serialized in 2021, as a cultural text, this article examines how bodily confrontation functions in place of spoken dialogue, enabling emotions, lived experiences, and needs for recognition that are difficult to articulate to become intelligible through physical encounters and reciprocal responses. It argues that when the understanding emerging from these encounters receives support from the groups concerned and develops into accountability, the rebuilding of relationships, and the renewal of communal life, the narrative's restorative orientation aligns substantially with RJ's emphasis on community participation and reintegration. Community is understood here both as a network of relationships affected by conflict and as an active participant in witnessing change, supporting acceptance, and sustaining restoration. To extend this argument, the article draws on sign language to demonstrate that dialogue does not require speech and considers international accounts of persons with disabilities participating in restorative processes. These accounts inform an examination of the potential of augmentative and alternative communication tools and artificial intelligence to support autonomous expression. Grounded in conceptual textual interpretation and a discussion of relevant literature, the article neither treats bodily confrontation as evidence of restorative effectiveness in practice nor advocates adopting fighting as an RJ intervention. Whether bodily interaction has restorative significance depends on voluntary and safe participation, opportunities to verify intended meanings, meaningful responses to harm, and the acceptance of responsibility. documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, Corporate Governance and the Limits of Algorithmic Consensus When ten artificial intelligence systems recommend the same decision, does their agreement provide ten independent assessments — or ten variations of the same underlying assumptions? This question lies at the centre of When Ten AI Systems Agree, Who Is Still Thinking?, an independent conceptual research paper by Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues within International Boardroom Studies and the Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP). As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into corporate decision-making, executive leadership, strategic planning, financial analysis and enterprise governance, organisations face an emerging challenge: distinguishing computational agreement from independently verified evidence. Large Language Models (LLMs), generative AI applications and multi-agent AI systems can produce consistent recommendations while relying on overlapping training data, shared information sources, correlated errors or common analytical assumptions. Apparent agreement may therefore create a level of confidence that the underlying evidence does not justify. The implications extend beyond technical model performance. They concern how boards of directors, chief executives, investment committees, corporate governance bodies and other institutional decision-makers interpret AI-generated information, challenge recommendations and translate approved decisions into accountable organisational action. Research Focus The paper introduces Artificial Consensus as a proposed institutional decision-making construct. Artificial Consensus describes circumstances in which multiple convergent AI-generated recommendations are interpreted as independent confirmation without adequate verification of their underlying evidentiary independence. The research brings together scholarship on: Artificial intelligence governance and trustworthy AI Large Language Models and correlated model errors Multi-agent systems and collective reasoning Algorithmic decision-making and automation bias Human–AI interaction, reliance and decision confidence Corporate governance, board oversight and executive accountability Strategic decision-making and evidence-based management Organisational decision processes and post-approval activation Existing machine-learning research demonstrates that different AI models can produce correlated errors and that multi-agent systems do not necessarily overcome incomplete information. Research on human–AI decision-making also examines how agreement and disagreement among AI systems may influence human confidence, conformity and verification behaviour. This paper extends that discussion into an institutional setting: what happens when AI-generated agreement becomes part of a consequential corporate decision? Scientific Contribution The central contribution is a conceptual framework distinguishing four elements that should not be treated as interchangeable. 1. Computational Convergence Multiple AI systems produce similar answers, assessments or recommendations. Agreement describes the outputs; it does not establish their correctness or independence. 2. Evidentiary Independence The underlying information, assumptions and potential failure modes must be examined. Different AI providers or model interfaces do not automatically constitute independent verification. 3. Institutional Decision Readiness A board or decision-making authority must determine whether material assumptions have been tested, contradictory evidence has been considered, and responsibilities and conditions have been made sufficiently explicit. 4. Post-Approval Decision Activation Formal authorisation must be distinguished from observable organisational action. A signed resolution does not establish that responsibility has been accepted, an executable first step has commenced or follow-up accountability exists. The framework thereby connects research on AI-generated recommendations with organisational governance without assuming that technical agreement automatically causes decision failure. Connection to Decision Non-Closure (DNC) The study forms part of the wider Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP), originated and directed by Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues. Decision Non-Closure (DNC) examines a specific post-approval condition: a formally authorised decision for which no traceable activation can be established within a defined observation period, provided the available evidence is sufficient to assess the relevant activity. The DNC framework identifies three proposed activation signals: Accepted ownership. A responsible person or function has accepted the first executable obligation. Concrete first action. An identifiable step towards implementation has commenced. Follow-up accountability. A mechanism exists to observe progress, identify blockages and establish responsibility for further action. The present study makes an important theoretical distinction. Artificial Consensus concerns the interpretation and scrutiny of AI-generated recommendations before formal approval. Decision Non-Closure concerns observable organisational activation after formal approval. The possible relationship between these stages is proposed for empirical investigation. It is not presented as an already established causal relationship. Research Methodology The paper develops a conceptual synthesis of contemporary research in machine learning, human–AI interaction and organisational decision-making. It draws on published studies examining correlated errors in large language models, the limitations of collective reasoning in multi-agent systems, AI majority effects on human decisions, model evaluation and governance-related behavioural mechanisms. Five falsifiable research propositions are developed. Two complementary empirical research designs are proposed. Study A — Human–AI Decision Experiment A controlled experimental design would examine whether the presentation of multiple agreeing AI recommendations changes perceived evidentiary independence, confidence, verification behaviour and the identification of unresolved assumptions. The proposed design distinguishes the number of recommendations from the actual independence of their supporting evidence. Study B — Longitudinal Organisational Decision Analysis A subsequent organisational study would examine formally approved decisions over defined observation periods. Its purpose would be to investigate whether unresolved evidentiary dependencies, decision conditions and accountability arrangements are associated with observable patterns of decision activation or potential Decision Non-Closure. The distinction between conceptual propositions and empirical results is maintained throughout the paper. Principal Research Outcomes Outcome 1 — AI agreement requires an independence assessment. A greater number of agreeing AI-generated recommendations does not necessarily provide a greater number of independent evidentiary confirmations. Model diversity, source provenance and error dependence must be examined in relation to the material decision. Outcome 2 — Effective human oversight requires substantive examination. Responsible human oversight is not established merely by placing a person at the final approval stage. Decision-makers require access to underlying assumptions, material contradictions and the evidence necessary to challenge automated recommendations. Outcome 3 — Formal approval and decision activation are distinct governance events. A decision may be authorised without establishing the operational responsibilities needed to begin implementation. Governance examination must distinguish evidentiary justification, institutional authority and observable action. Outcome 4 — The relationship between Artificial Consensus and Decision Non-Closure is empirically testable. The proposed framework identifies specific behavioural, documentary and organisational variables that future studies can measure. The relationship may be supported, limited or rejected by subsequent evidence. Relevance to International Corporate Governance The research addresses questions relevant to organisations integrating artificial intelligence into consequential decision processes, including: Corporate strategy and capital allocation; mergers and acquisitions; investment committee decisions; financial and operational analysis; multinational enterprises; family-owned businesses; institutional investment; board accountability; and the governance of AI-supported executive decisions. Its implications also extend to AI assurance, evidence provenance, algorithmic accountability, model risk management and the design of human oversight within organisations. The paper does not propose that artificial intelligence should be excluded from corporate governance. Instead, it examines how AI-generated information can be used without confusing apparent consensus with independent scrutiny. The governing question is not simply whether ten systems agree. It is what their agreement actually establishes — and who remains responsible for the decision that follows. About the Author Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues is an independent researcher and author, the scientific originator of Decision Non-Closure (DNC), and Research Director of the Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP) within International Boardroom Studies. Her research examines the institutional conditions under which consequential decisions become vulnerable to unresolved assumptions, competing interpretations of authority, inadequate scrutiny and gaps in accountability. Her interdisciplinary work brings together organisational decision theory, international corporate governance, institutional behaviour and emerging AI-supported decision systems.
