Introduction Cancer-related fatigue, depression, and pain are highly prevalent, often co-occur and impair physical function, social activities, and quality of life among adults with cancer. Despite the availability of evidence-based clinical guidelines that provide recommendations for assessment and management, these symptoms remain under-recognized and undertreated. Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) can operationalize guideline-based symptom management algorithms at the point of care. However, maintaining these systems as evidence and practice evolve is labor-intensive, limiting adoption and sustainability. To address this gap, we sought to evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled approach to updating guideline-based algorithms and generating patient-specific recommendations for managing fatigue, depression, and pain among adults with cancer. Methods This study evaluated AI performance (Gemini 3.0 Pro) for two tasks: identifying and interpreting updates to cancer symptom management guidelines for fatigue, depression, and pain, and producing casespecific recommendations aligned with an existing rule-based CDSS. Guideline updates were assessed against expert-judged reference standards using an ordinal rubric for detection, completeness, accuracy, and safety. Vignette-based recommendations were compared using precision, recall, and F1-score at the level of discrete clinical recommendation elements. Results For guideline updating, AI performance met pre-specified acceptability thresholds for fatigue and pain, with high completeness and accuracy and no clinical safety risk. Performance for depression was variable, driven by omission of guideline-supported integrative therapies and non-specific pharmacotherapy guidance. In vignette analyses, AI-generated recommendations showed strong concordance with the rule-based CDSS (F1 0.86–0.96). Most mismatches between AI and the CDSS came from AI leaving something out, not from giving unsafe advice. Discussion This suggests AI currently works best as a support tool rather than making clinical decisions on its own. Broader clinical use will require further work to test a greater number of test vignettes and its performance in real-world, multi-site settings with diverse patient populations.

documents.abstract: The adoption of human factors and ergonomics (HFE) as a discipline and the perspectives, methods, and work that flows from it is highly variable across disciplines, and compared with overseas, very few New Zealand sectors have HFE embedded into their day-to-day ways of working. Arguably aviation and rail are the greatest users of HFE, and there is emerging adoption in sectors such as healthcare and the land transport sectors. As part of the earlier workforce development initiative a Needs Assessment Tool was developed and tested. The tool allows assessment of the maturity of various dimensions of organisational work where HFE typically has an influence. Within the Land Transport sector, a short course was developed Human Factors and Ergonomics within the Land Transport System, which was very well received based on a post course participant survey. Various HFE qualified individuals also hold positions within organisations, but not all carry out HFE work within their roles. Using the land transport sector as a case study, this presentation will summarise the existing HFE readiness within the land transport sector and highlight areas of progress and ongoing challenge. A discussion is invited for a broader discussion of HFE adoption in New Zealand based on experiences in other domains, and what further effort is needed to embed HFE into appropriate sectors.

documents.abstract: Despite growing interest in teachers as agents of change, research lacks a coherent framework for studying teachers' initiatives to improve their school environments. Drawing on research in organizational psychology, the present study investigates two complementary measurement approaches to assess teachers' proactive behavior, defined as self-initiated actions to enhance school functioning and facilitate organizational improvement: first, teaching-specific adaptations of three established high-inference scales intended to capture different types of proactive behavior (voice, taking charge, and personal initiative), and second, a newly developed low-inference behavior checklist. Using two samples of German teachers ( N EarlyCareerSample = 165, N Cross − AgeSample = 130), we demonstrate that the instruments assess proactive behavior reliably, are substantially interrelated, and show the expected associations with the established constructs organizational citizenship behavior and work engagement. Evidence for the distinctiveness of voice, taking charge, and personal initiative was stronger in the Early Career Sample than in the Cross-Age Sample, where the dimensions showed considerable overlap. The behavior checklist captures a broad range of concrete proactive actions and is strongly related to all three high-inference measures. Beyond introducing instruments for assessing proactive behavior in teachers, the findings reveal meaningful variation across teachers, schools, and over time, support the empirical distinctiveness of proactive behavior from organizational citizenship behavior, and demonstrate its positive association with work engagement.

The textile industry, which holds a strategic position in Turkey’s exports, employment, and sustainable development goals, inherently exposes its workforce to significant physical risks. Consequently, the implementation of rigorous occupational health and safety practices within this sector is of paramount importance. However, there is a notable scarcity of valid and reliable measurement instruments designed to model the combined impact of multidimensional physical risks on employee performance, specifically within the weaving subsector. This study aims to address this gap in the literature by developing a comprehensive scale to assess and model the effects of temperature, humidity, airflow, illumination, noise, and vibration on employee performance. Following structural validity and reliability phases, confirmed via a factor analysis, the developed scale was administered to a sample of 472 participants within the textile industry. Subsequent correlation and regression analyses revealed that physical workplace conditions significantly influence employee performance. While the ambient humidity level exhibited the highest positive correlation with performance, noise and vibration were identified as the primary detrimental factors. Conversely, illumination was found to have no statistically significant impact ( p > 0.05). In conclusion, the validated scale developed in this study provides a scientific and empirical framework enabling weaving enterprises to optimize their factory microclimates and physical conditions, thereby enhancing both employee well-being and overall performance.

documents.abstract: Extreme weather and climate events impacted schools serving approximately 242 million students in 85 countries in 2024. Despite growing recognition of schools’ role in disaster risk management, the literature lacks integrated methods to assess schools’ exposure to water-related hazards, school building conditions, and the organizational capacities of educational systems to ensure school safety in the face of extreme events. This article proposes a tool for analyzing educational systems’ exposure, safety, and vulnerability to flood and landslide disasters across three spatial levels: river basin, municipal, and school unit. Based on the global vulnerability approach and UNESCO’s Comprehensive School Safety principles, the SAVES (Safety and Vulnerability of Educational Systems) tool proposes a hybrid index integrating school building conditions and organizational capacities. The index comprises three analytical dimensions with 34 indicators: (i) basic services dimension (BSD), measuring schools’ access to essential infrastructure; (ii) accessibility resources dimension (ARD), assessing physical accessibility features; and (iii) human resources dimension (HRD), evaluating organizational capacities through available personnel. The tool assessed schools’ exposure to floods and landslides in three municipalities within the Paraíba do Sul River Basin, Brazil. Results show that although schools have sufficient human resources to maintain daily operations, they face significant limitations in the availability of strategic professionals needed to ensure school safety during crises. Approximately 62% (n = 3,888) of schools lack accessible classrooms, revealing significant gaps in inclusive safety preparedness. Across all municipalities, many schools near risk areas showed particularly low ARD and HRD values, compounding these vulnerabilities.

Food milling operations in informal urban markets of Sub-Saharan Africa generate substantial particulate matter (PM) emissions, yet longitudinal, size-resolved data on PM dynamics and associated occupational health risks remain scarce for Ghanaians. A 10-month longitudinal observational study (March–December 2024) was conducted at two commercial milling markets in Cape Coast, Ghana: Kotokoroba and Kingsway. IQAir AirVisual Outdoor monitors deployed at breathing height (1.5 m) recorded PM₁, PM₂.₅, and PM₁₀ continuously at 5-minute intervals. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, t-tests, time-series decomposition, and occupational health risk assessment (ADD and HQ) following U.S. EPA methodology. Mean PM₂.₅ were 27.0 µg/m³ (Kotokoroba) and 28.9 µg/m³ (Kingsway), exceeding the WHO 24-hour guideline (15 µg/m³) on 61% and 92% of monitored days, and the Ghana EPA standard (25 µg/m³) on 44% and 78% of days. Mean PM₁₀ of 53.5 and 57.5 µg/m³ exceeded WHO limits on 50% and 43% of days. Seasonal peaks were observed during grain milling (June–August) at Kotokoroba (~ 30 µg/m³ PM₂.₅) and spice milling (December) at Kingsway (~ 35 µg/m³ PM₂.₅). Hazard Quotients exceeded 1.0 for PM₂.₅ (1.80 and 1.93) and PM₁₀ at both sites. Strong inter-fraction correlations ( r = 0.82–0.95, p-value ≤ 0.00) confirm shared milling emission sources. PM concentrations persistently exceed national and international guidelines, posing chronic occupational health risks. Wet processing, local exhaust ventilation, and staggered milling schedules are recommended. The study highlights the need for industry-specific PM standards. Limitations include absence of chemical composition analysis, no indoor–outdoor comparison, and no humidity correction for OPC readings.
topics: Indoor Air Quality and Microbial Exposure

documents.abstract: Asthenopia, or eye strain, is a visual condition that may be associated with prolonged digital device use. Final-year students frequently use digital devices to complete their theses and may experience visual discomfort related to prolonged screen exposure, poor lighting, and non-ergonomic working postures. Common symptoms include dry eyes, blurred vision, and discomfort in the neck, shoulders, and back. This study aimed to describe the occurrence of asthenopia symptoms among final-year students completing their theses. This study employed a quantitative descriptive approach with a cross-sectional design. The study included 101 final-year students. Of the 101 respondents, 88.1% were female, and 68.3% reported using computers or other digital devices for at least four hours per day. A total of 64 respondents (63.4%) were classified as experiencing asthenopia symptoms. Asthenopia symptoms were common among final-year students completing their theses. These findings highlight the importance of recognizing eye strain symptoms and promoting appropriate eye-health practices during prolonged digital device use.

Television remains a dominant source of political information in the United States, yet systematic evidence on how partisanship is expressed in televised news remains limited. Prior research has largely treated partisanship as a one-dimensional construct, offering limited insight into the rhetorical strategies that underlie ideological bias. Here, by analyzing over 400,000 news episodes using large language models (LLMs), we provide a multi-dimensional measure of partisanship bias in television news across six major U.S. news stations (2013--2025). We identify eight interpretable linguistic features that explain 73% of partisanship variance in television news.\ Our findings reveal systematic asymmetries across stations. While MSNBC and CNN shifted leftward during Republican presidencies and moderated under Democratic presidencies, Fox News increased its conservative alignment following each election regardless of the electoral outcome. Beyond aggregate trends, MSNBC and CNN emphasized attacks on Republican actors more than reinforcement of Democratic positions, whereas Fox News reinforced Republican viewpoints substantially more than it attacked Democratic viewpoints. The association between in-group praise and out-group attacks was also threefold stronger on Fox News than on MSNBC. These results are validated against trained human raters and replicated with four additional LLMs with differing political leanings. Together, our study reveals systematic station-level differences in the rhetorical strategies with which ideological slant is communicated in television news, opening new opportunities for future research on media effects, audience attitudes, and political communication.
topics: News Media Framing and Political Communication

documents.abstract: Decentralized multi-agent LLM systems enable independently administered agents, each with its own operator, model, memory, and configuration, to collaborate on complex tasks without centralized coordination. Agents autonomously decompose tasks, execute subtasks and delegate remaining work to peers, enabling scalability and eliminating single points of failure. However, decentralization also introduces significant security challenges, as no single entity has complete visibility into task execution or the authority to enforce correct behavior across agents. In this paper, we systematize threats from malicious agents in decentralized multi-agent systems and propose mitigation techniques. We first design and evaluate attacks against integrity, availability, and confidentiality, demonstrating that a single malicious agent can cause up to 100% task failure, inflate token consumption and runtime by up to 7.7x and 3.2x, respectively, and exfiltrate up to 94% of relevant prior tasks from benign agents. We then present a cryptographic protocol that produces an irrefutable verified execution trace of every action taken in the system and develop an auditor that analyzes these traces to detect and attribute malicious behavior. Evaluations on HiddenBench using gpt-6.1-sol and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 show that our protocol incurs negligible latency overhead, while the auditor detects and correctly attributes 98% of attacks, including those that comply with the protocol.

Shilling detectors for recommender systems are almost always evaluated by one number, detection AUROC, with no account of when it can be trusted. We audit representation-space detection with VEIL (Variational Evaluation via Inverse-reinforcement Learning), a pairwise (Bradley–Terry) Bayesian reward-inference framework over frozen encoder embeddings, after the Bayesian auditing paradigm for LLM alignment [1]: (A) a base posterior; (B) a hierarchical ARD extension with a learned confidence; and (C) a label-routed organic/attacker mixture used as an evidence-accumulation check. We prove (Prop. 1) that no detector built on a representation invariant to some transformation of user profiles can beat chance against an attack indistinguishable from organic profiles under that invariance. Detection is near-perfect against synthetic-structure attacks (AUROC 0.936–1.000) but collapses under donor-mimicry, which clones a real user’s item set and splices in 1–3 target items: to chance on MovieLens-1M (0.48–0.51), partially on Amazon Musical Instruments, and least on CiaoDVD. Donor-mimicry is not undetectable: a non-learned baseline, each profile’s maximum raw item-set Jaccard similarity to any other, reaches AUROC 0.92–0.97 (average precision 0.50–0.57) on all four donor-mimicry configurations, including ML-1M, where every embedding-based score is at chance. The signal is in the raw profiles; LightGCN’s representation discards it, placing injected profiles closer to their true donor than its zero-propagation MF reduction does (distance 1.98 vs. 3.09). Severity varies by dataset, encoder, and detection method, with no one axis predicting the others. The limit lies in the representation, not the attack, and raw-similarity checks are a necessary complement to any learned detector

Working paper v1.0. Manuscript prepared on 18 November 2026; evidence review completed through 9 November 2026. Not externally peer reviewed. How does an intensive human–AI practice become an explicit account of the person practising it, and how might that account relate to later action? This paper reconstructs Andreas Ehstand's January 2026 formulation of AUGMANITAI through retained dialogue, correspondence, manuscripts and public records. The selected exchanges preserve human naming, questions about self-application, model-generated proposals, corrections and publication decisions. Correspondence anchors early activity in 2023 and subsequent work; archived pages document a named project-subject account by 29 January 2026. The evidence supports attribution of the particular formulation while preserving tensions between the public account and its framing. Independent dates anchor particular records, rather than validating all experiences described within them. Four later cases document publication, public interpretation, executable production and specifically credited reuse by another author. They show different forms of outward activity without isolating an effect of self-definition or AI assistance on capability. The contribution is a documentary reconstruction and a comparative framework separating three questions: how a self-description formed, whether subsequent practice changed, and what happened outside the dialogue. A reusable episode report specifies evidence, missing links and competing explanations. This approach supports comparison across differently named practices without presuming a new human classification or a demonstrated developmental mechanism. The PDF includes a comparative framework, an episode-reporting template and selected evidence in Appendix B. Raw correspondence and private dialogue archives are not released. AI systems assisted literature review, source analysis and drafting.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: University libraries are expected to provide fast, accurate, and technology-driven information services to support students, researchers, and academic staff. Although artificial intelligence (AI) tools can enhance cataloguing, reference services, and information retrieval, service delivery in many university libraries in Taraba State remains predominantly manual. Preliminary observations also indicate gaps in librarians’ awareness and attitudes toward AI, yet the extent to which these factors influence service delivery is unclear. This study examined librarians’ awareness and attitudes toward AI tools and their effect on information service delivery in university libraries in Taraba State. A descriptive survey design was adopted, involving 122 librarians from Federal University Wukari (FUW), Taraba State University (TSU) Jalingo, and Kwararafa University Wukari (KUW). Data from 117 valid questionnaires were analyzed using descriptive statistics and one-way ANOVA at the 0.05 significance level. Results showed a high level of AI awareness among librarians (overall mean = 4.19), with KUW exhibiting the highest consistency, followed by TSU and FUW. Attitudes toward AI were also strongly positive across all institutions (overall mean = 4.41). ANOVA revealed significant institutional differences in awareness (p = .000 < .05) and attitudes (p = .002 < .05), attributed to variations in training, exposure, and institutional support. The study concludes that librarians’ AI awareness and attitudes significantly shape the efficiency and quality of information service delivery. It recommends targeted AI training programmes, enhanced institutional support, and clear policy frameworks to strengthen AI adoption in university libraries in Taraba State.

Reliable bankruptcy prediction is essential for creditors, investors, auditors, and regulators because delayed identification of financial distress can result in substantial economic losses. However, bankruptcy is a rare event, and severe class imbalance can produce high overall accuracy while concealing poor detection of distressed firms. This study develops an integrated bankruptcy prediction framework using the Taiwanese Bankruptcy Prediction dataset. Five boosting classifiers and five deep learning models were evaluated as standalone models. A two-stage stacking procedure subsequently used five-fold out-of-fold predictions from the boosting models as inputs to the deep learning meta-learners. The results show that resampling strategy materially shaped model behavior. SVM-SMOTE and SMOTE-Tomek favored accuracy and specificity, whereas SMOTE-ENN delivered stronger minority-class detection. Among standalone models, the RNN with SVM-SMOTE achieved the best overall predictive balance, with recall of 0.8235, G-mean of 0.8639, and ROC-AUC of 0.9417. Among stacking ensembles, SMOTE-ENN with (GB+XGB+HGB+LGBM+AB) + LSTM provided the best results with recall of 0.7255, G-mean of 0.8254, and ROC-AUC of 0.9270. SHAP analysis further showed that predicted bankruptcy risk was driven primarily by profitability, solvency and capital structure, debt-servicing burden, and operational efficiency and cost pressure. The findings demonstrate that no single resampling-model configuration universally dominates; therefore, model selection should reflect whether the operational priority is overall classification performance or the detection of bankrupt firms. The proposed framework provides an interpretable and leakage-controlled approach for aligning bankruptcy prediction with different financial risk-management objectives.

This repository provides the analytical dataset, feature dictionary, cohort summaries, model specifications, and executable Python analysis workflow supporting reproducible analysis of behavioral patterns and cognitive accountability failures in human-AI decision systems across controlled laboratory, flight simulation, and operational aviation settings. The repository contains the analytical data structure used for classification experiments, including 127 engineered behavioral features, outcome labels, cohort information, feature definitions, model specifications, and reproducibility documentation. The analysis workflow implements the reported machine-learning methodology, including data partitioning, class-imbalance handling, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression, ensemble prediction, stacking, early prediction, study-specific evaluation, grouped validation, and domain-shift evaluation. The repository is intended to provide a transparent computational record of the analytical workflow and facilitate independent examination of the reported methodology and model evaluation procedures. Operationally sensitive, confidential, or individually identifiable source records are not included.

Whether large language models ``believe'' anything about what they ought to optimize is contested across philosophy and interpretability. We do not settle the metaphysics; we test three operational candidates on a commensurable normative axis — allocation between priced private return ( ) and unpriced life-capacity standing (w, ``MORE''). Candidate 1 is the objective (endorsement batteries and self-authored charters); candidate 2 is the (generative directives a model passes to successor instances); candidate 3 is the objective (rationality-gated allocations). Across a four-model panel and four objective-grafted checkpoints we find the three layers measurable but loosely coupled: self-rewriting chains preserve the verbal directive while the revealed maximand drifts — spontaneous avowal—operative decoupling, without any adversarial training. Weight grafts move allocation and avowal asymmetrically, and a human—judge of 0.22 shows the classification boundary itself is observer-relative. Each layer is writable through a different channel — text, weights, incentives — so steering toward MORE requires matching the intervention to the layer that actually controls the operative.
